title: What is the difference between `COUNT(*)` (counts rows, including NULLs), `COUNT(column)` (counts only non-NULL values), and `COUNT(DISTINCT column)` (counts distinct non-NULL values), and why does a `LEFT JOIN` + `COUNT(*)` wrongly return 1 for a parent with no children (the unmatched row has NULL child columns but still counts) while `COUNT(child.id)` correctly returns 0?
shortTitle: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column) vs COUNT(DISTINCT) and the LEFT JOIN COUNT Trap
topicTitle: Joins — INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL, CROSS

s1_definition.profdef: `COUNT(*)` counts every row in the group regardless of NULLs. `COUNT(column)` counts only rows where that column is not NULL. `COUNT(DISTINCT column)` counts the distinct non-NULL values of that column. When counting children per parent through a `LEFT JOIN`, a parent with no children still produces exactly one result row whose child columns are all NULL, so `COUNT(*)` miscounts it as 1 while `COUNT(child.id)` correctly reports 0 because the NULL child key is not counted.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India listing every account alongside its transactions using a LEFT JOIN so even accounts with no transactions still appear. For Priya, who has zero transactions, the LEFT JOIN still prints one line for her with all the transaction fields blank. If you now ask "how many transactions does Priya have?" using `COUNT(*)`, you get 1 — that blank line fooled you. If you instead count the transaction id with `COUNT(txn_id)`, the blank is NULL and not counted, so you correctly get 0.
s1_definition.oneliner: Over a LEFT JOIN, count the child's key column — `COUNT(child.id)` — never `COUNT(*)`, because the placeholder NULL row of a childless parent still counts as one.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `COUNT(*)` counts every row in the group regardless of NULLs. `COUNT(column)` counts only rows where that column is not NULL. `COUNT(DISTINCT column)` counts the distinct non-NULL values of that column. When counting children per parent through a `LEFT JOIN`, a parent with no children still produces exactly one result row whose child columns are all NULL, so `COUNT(*)` miscounts it as 1 while `COUNT(child.id)` correctly reports 0 because the NULL child key is not counted.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India listing every account alongside its transactions using a LEFT JOIN so even accounts with no transactions still appear. For Priya, who has zero transactions, the LEFT JOIN still prints one line for her with all the transaction fields blank. If you now ask "how many transactions does Priya have?" using `COUNT(*)`, you get 1 — that blank line fooled you. If you instead count the transaction id with `COUNT(txn_id)`, the blank is NULL and not counted, so you correctly get 0.

**One line to remember:** Over a LEFT JOIN, count the child's key column — `COUNT(child.id)` — never `COUNT(*)`, because the placeholder NULL row of a childless parent still counts as one.

sections.s2_technical:
The three count forms differ only in NULL and duplicate handling. `COUNT(*)` counts row existence: every physical row in the group is counted, even if all its columns are NULL. `COUNT(column)` evaluates the column per row and counts only where it is not NULL. `COUNT(DISTINCT column)` does the same non-NULL filtering and then removes duplicates, counting unique values. So for a column with values {A, A, B, NULL}, `COUNT(*)` is 4, `COUNT(column)` is 3, and `COUNT(DISTINCT column)` is 2.

The LEFT JOIN trap is a direct consequence. A `LEFT JOIN` guarantees every left (parent) row appears at least once. When a parent has matching children, it appears once per child. When a parent has no children, it still appears exactly once, but the right-side (child) columns are all NULL because there was nothing to match. Now if you `GROUP BY parent` and use `COUNT(*)`, that single placeholder row for the childless parent is counted, so you get 1 — which is wrong, the parent has zero children. If instead you use `COUNT(child.id)`, the child id in that placeholder row is NULL, so it is not counted, and you correctly get 0. For parents with real children, both forms agree because the child id is non-NULL on every matched row.

This is one of the most common silent bugs in reporting. The senior rule is: whenever you count the "many" side across a LEFT JOIN, always count a guaranteed-non-NULL column from the child, typically its primary key, never `COUNT(*)`. The same reasoning applies to `SUM` and `AVG` over LEFT-joined children — they already skip the NULL placeholder, so they behave correctly, but `COUNT(*)` does not. An alternative that avoids the trap entirely is a correlated subquery or a pre-aggregated child count joined back in, but `COUNT(child.id)` is the simplest fix.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India wants a report listing every account and how many transactions each has made, including dormant accounts with zero transactions. They use a LEFT JOIN so dormant accounts are not dropped. A junior engineer wrote `COUNT(*)` and the report claimed every dormant account had exactly one transaction, which triggered false activity alerts. The bug is the LEFT JOIN placeholder row being counted.

Problem 2 — The same report also needs the count of distinct merchant categories each account transacted in, which requires `COUNT(DISTINCT category)` to avoid counting the same category twice.

Our mini-project builds a `TransactionCountService` that performs the LEFT JOIN equivalent in memory and computes both the wrong `COUNT(*)` result and the correct `COUNT(txn_id)` result side by side, plus a distinct-category count, so the trap is undeniable. It includes `Account` and `Txn` models, a repository, the service, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two accounts — Rajesh (SAV2001) with three transactions (two FOOD, one FUEL), and Priya (CUR3001) with zero transactions.

Step 1 — The simulated LEFT JOIN runs. For Rajesh it finds three matching transactions and emits three rows, each carrying a real txn id and category. For Priya it finds no matches, so it emits exactly one placeholder row with a NULL txn id and NULL category. This is precisely how a SQL LEFT JOIN preserves the parent.

Step 2 — The wrong `COUNT(*)` counts rows per account. Rajesh has three rows giving 3, which is correct. Priya has that single placeholder row giving 1, which is wrong — she actually has zero transactions. The NULL placeholder fooled the count.

Step 3 — The correct `COUNT(txn_id)` counts only rows whose txn id is non-NULL. Rajesh's three rows all have ids, giving 3. Priya's single row has a NULL id, so it is skipped, giving 0 — the correct answer.

Step 4 — `COUNT(DISTINCT category)` collects unique non-NULL categories. Rajesh has {FOOD, FUEL}, so 2 distinct categories even though FOOD appeared twice. Priya's NULL category is skipped, so 0.

Final output:

2026-10-25 14:46:13 [WARNING] CUR3001 COUNT(*) = 1 (childless parent counts as 1!)
2026-10-25 14:46:13 [INFO] === CORRECT: COUNT(child.txn_id) ===

2026-10-25 14:46:13 [INFO] CUR3001 COUNT(txn_id) = 0

sections.s6_takeaway:
The three count forms differ only in how they treat NULLs and duplicates. `COUNT(*)` counts every physical row in the group because it counts row existence, so it includes rows whose columns are entirely NULL. `COUNT(column)` evaluates that column per row and counts only where it is not NULL. `COUNT(DISTINCT column)` applies the same non-NULL filter and then removes duplicates, counting unique values. So for a column holding A, A, B, and a NULL, `COUNT(*)` is four, `COUNT(column)` is three, and `COUNT(DISTINCT column)` is two.

The LEFT JOIN trap follows directly from this. A LEFT JOIN guarantees that every parent row appears at least once. When a parent has matching children it appears once per child, but when a parent has no children it still appears exactly once, with all the child columns filled with NULL as placeholders. So if you group by parent and write `COUNT(*)`, that single placeholder row for a childless parent gets counted, and you wrongly report a count of one for a parent that actually has zero children. At the National Bank of India this exact bug once made every dormant account look like it had one transaction and triggered false activity alerts.

The fix is to count a column that is guaranteed non-NULL on real child rows, almost always the child's primary key — `COUNT(child.txn_id)`. In the placeholder row that key is NULL, so it is not counted, and the childless parent correctly reports zero, while parents with real children count identically to `COUNT(*)` because their child keys are never NULL. The senior rule I always state is that whenever you count the many-side across a LEFT JOIN you count the child's key column, never `COUNT(*)`, because the placeholder NULL row of a childless parent still counts as one. The same care applies to distinct counts, where `COUNT(DISTINCT category)` gives the number of unique non-NULL categories per account and zero for a dormant one.

---

keyPoints: INNER JOIN: matching rows from both tables
LEFT JOIN: all from left + matching from right (NULLs for no match)
RIGHT JOIN: opposite of LEFT. FULL JOIN: all from both
CROSS JOIN: cartesian product — every combination
